title: 'The Gen AI LLM benchmarking war starts here': Harvey releases new evaluation framework
author: Legal IT Insider · Neil Cameron

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s distinction between generic benchmark scores and task-specific legal performance, and materially develops it by describing real-world task construction, tailored rubrics, penalties for hallucinations and separate sourcing assessment. However, it does not itself demonstrate that average scores conceal complete-task failure, and Harvey’s superiority claim is reported rather than independently validated.
qs: One of the challenges of evaluating LLMs on the tasks that lawyers do is that they are too complicated to be graded by multiple choice or 'one-size-fits-all' criteria.
Harvey also benchmarks the viability of a model's sourcing of its answers, with a high score for correct sourcing and low score for lack of traceability and validation.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source accepts task-specific evaluation as more realistic than uniform legal tests and materially strengthens the cluster’s reproducibility concerns by questioning the subjective, inconsistently coded time-entry data underlying Harvey’s task construction.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified treatment of benchmarking: it explains BigLaw Bench’s task-specific evaluation design and sourcing checks while carefully attributing performance superiority to Harvey rather than treating it as independent proof of legal performance or durable defensibility.
qs: One of the challenges of evaluating LLMs on the tasks that lawyers do is that they are too complicated to be graded by multiple choice or 'one-size-fits-all' criteria.
Harvey says it outperforms each of the leading foundation models.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s caution that benchmark results are bounded and should not independently justify deployment. It stresses that useful legal-AI evaluation requires standardised taxonomies, consistent application and additional objective criteria for accuracy and usefulness.
qs: Whilst they may be useful in comparing, as Harvey states, the extent to which 'models can contribute to real, high-value legal work', the degree to which it can be of any additional assistance is then reliant on the level of standardisation of, and compliance to, the 'relevant taxonomies' to which Harvey then refers.
As useful as that approach may be, we will still need some additional objective criteria for measuring the accuracy and usefulness of the LLM model response.

kp.k: Harvey launched a real-world legal-task benchmarking framework
kp.d: Legal IT Insider reports that Harvey released BigLaw Bench on 3 September 2024 to quantify large language model performance on real-world legal tasks. Harvey presents it as a supplement to prior evaluations focused on legal reasoning in more structured settings.
qs: Gen AI startup Harvey has released a benchmarking framework for quantitatively evaluating the performance of large language models on real-world legal tasks.
The model supplements, it says, prior work that measures LLM legal reasoning in more structured settings.

kp.k: Time entries are converted into classified benchmark tasks
kp.d: Harvey derives benchmark tasks from lawyers' time entries, then classifies them using taxonomies including practice area, transactional or litigation work, and the portion of a matter represented. This design is intended to address legal tasks too complex for multiple-choice or uniform grading.
qs: One of the challenges of evaluating LLMs on the tasks that lawyers do is that they are too complicated to be graded by multiple choice or 'one-size-fits-all' criteria.

Harvey has instead converted time entries into model-based tasks, which are then divided by other relevant taxonomies such as practice area, type of work (transactional/litigation etc) and the portion of a matter that the task would take.

kp.k: Task-specific rubrics reward requirements and penalise defects
kp.d: Harvey uses task-specific rubrics identifying both required and prohibited features. The reported scoring method awards positive points for satisfied criteria, deducts points for defects including hallucinations, and divides the combined score by the points available for the task.
qs: Harvey then developed rubrics to evaluate each task – an objective criteria needed to accomplish a given task.
Penalties are given for incorrect tone, length, irrelevant material, toxicity, and hallucinations.
The rubrics must capture everything a model MUST do and everything it MUST avoid.
The overall score is computed by taking the combination of positive and negative points and dividing it by the number of points available for a task.

kp.k: Source traceability and validation are separately benchmarked
kp.d: The framework assesses whether a model's answers are supported by viable sources. Correct sourcing earns a high score, while answers lacking traceability and validation receive a low score; Neil Cameron endorses source confirmation as an essential benchmark criterion.
qs: Harvey also benchmarks the viability of a model's sourcing of its answers, with a high score for correct sourcing and low score for lack of traceability and validation.
The fundamental importance of source confirmation is surely uncontroversial and vital to any benchmark.

kp.k: Harvey claims superiority over leading foundation models
kp.d: The article reports Harvey's vendor claim that its system performs better than each leading foundation model. The document supplies no comparative scores, model list, sample size, or independent validation for that claim.
qs: Harvey says it outperforms each of the leading foundation models.

kp.k: Benchmark examples cover litigation and transactional work
kp.d: Harvey provides example tasks from litigation and transactional categories, while a broader set of BigLaw Bench exemplar tasks and their rubrics is available on GitHub. The article does not state the complete benchmark's task count or dataset size.
qs: Here it provides an example task from both the litigation and transactional categories for reference.
A more comprehensive description of exemplar tasks sampled from BigLaw Bench, including associated rubrics, can be found on GitHub.

kp.k: Legal AI buyers need standardised comparative evaluation
kp.d: The article situates BigLaw Bench alongside standardisation efforts by Stanford University and the UK Legal IT Innovators Group. These initiatives are described as attempts to help buyers compare generative-AI outputs, while Cameron argues that law firms need an industry-wide, non-partisan benchmark.
qs: This release follows efforts from Stanford University and the UK Legal IT Innovators Group led by CMS' head of innovation John Craske to drive standardisation and benchmarking in order to better enable buyers of Gen AI tools to compare their output.
As we noted in the LITI Gen AI in law report, law firms badly need an industry-wide, non-partisan Gen AI LLM benchmarking model.

kp.k: Competing benchmarks may precede an industry standard
kp.d: Cameron predicts that a broadly accepted legal-AI benchmark will emerge only after competing frameworks undergo reconciliation, rationalisation, and consolidation. He characterises Harvey's release as the opening phase of a benchmarking “war,” not as an established industry standard.
qs: This will probably only truly emerge after a period of emergence of competing benchmark models followed by reconciliation, rationalisation and consolidation.
So, the first phase of the Gen AI LLM benchmark 'war' starts here.

kp.k: Cameron questions time-entry data as an objective foundation
kp.d: Cameron argues that raw time-entry data contains embedded subjectivity. Although classifications such as areas of law, work types, UTBMS, and J-Codes can aid comparison, attorneys may apply them inaccurately or manipulate them for commercial purposes, limiting benchmark reliability.
qs: The Harvey approach established two clear fundamental criteria – time entry comparison and source confirmation.
The comparative time entry concept is more problematic.
As anyone who has tried to analyse raw time entry data for useful 'information' (whether manually or using GenAI) will attest, it is fraught with it own baked in subjectivities.

While attempts to normalise such data, such as 'area of law', 'work types', UTBMS and J-Codes, can provide some objective basis for comparison and analysis, these are often treated with slapdash accuracy by careless attorneys, and by more imaginative attorneys as much as a challenge to exploit for commercial purposes, as they are for support and enlightenment.

kp.k: Benchmark usefulness depends on taxonomy standardisation and compliance
kp.d: Cameron conditionally accepts that time-entry-derived tasks may indicate whether models can contribute to high-value legal work, but says their additional value depends on consistent taxonomies and attorney compliance. He recommends further objective criteria for measuring response accuracy and usefulness.
qs: Whilst they may be useful in comparing, as Harvey states, the extent to which 'models can contribute to real, high-value legal work', the degree to which it can be of any additional assistance is then reliant on the level of standardisation of, and compliance to, the 'relevant taxonomies' to which Harvey then refers.
As useful as that approach may be, we will still need some additional objective criteria for measuring the accuracy and usefulness of the LLM model response.
That is the Holy Grail, and for that we eagerly await the next steps.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey claims its framework measures LLM performance on real-world legal tasks and that its own system outperforms leading foundation models; Neil Cameron predicts competing benchmarks will precede an industry-wide standard.
pts.d: The report describes Harvey's BigLaw Bench as supplementing structured legal-reasoning assessments with tasks derived from lawyers' time entries, task-specific scoring rubrics and assessment of answer sourcing. Harvey's comparative-performance claim is explicitly a vendor claim. Cameron argues that law firms need a non-partisan benchmark for the usefulness and accuracy of generative AI legal advice, and predicts that such a standard will probably emerge through competition followed by reconciliation and consolidation. He regards source confirmation as essential but says time-entry-based comparisons remain dependent on the quality and consistency of underlying classifications and require additional objective criteria. The source's claims concern measuring and comparing AI's contribution to legal work, rather than predictions about lawyer displacement or quantified productivity gains.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of Harvey's benchmark methodology and references to exemplar tasks, alongside Cameron's experience-based critique; the article supplies no numerical comparative results.
pts.d: The report explains that Harvey converts time entries into tasks classified by practice area, work type and matter portion, then scores responses against positive and negative rubric criteria. It also assesses sourcing and traceability. Litigation and transactional examples are referenced, with further exemplar tasks and rubrics available on GitHub. These descriptions provide the stated methodological basis for assessing performance, but the supplied text includes no scores, sample sizes or independent validation of Harvey's superiority claim. Cameron invokes practical experience analysing time-entry data and points to subjectivity, inaccurate coding and commercial incentives as limitations. His forecast of benchmark consolidation is an analytical expectation, not a data-backed forecast in this document.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The framework and vendor performance claim are current as of 3 September 2024; an industry standard is an undated, qualified future prospect.
pts.d: The article reports a framework already released at publication. Cameron frames benchmark competition as beginning at that point and offers no deadline for consolidation. He presents industry adoption as a possibility rather than an established outcome. He conditions the usefulness of time-entry comparisons on standardisation of, and compliance with, relevant taxonomies, while maintaining that additional objective response-quality criteria are still needed.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Law firms and buyers of generative AI tools are the principal intended beneficiaries, through better comparison of tools' legal-work outputs.
pts.d: The report places Harvey's release alongside other standardisation efforts intended to help buyers compare generative AI output. Cameron specifically identifies law firms' need for a non-partisan assessment of legal AI usefulness and accuracy. The benchmark covers litigation and transactional tasks, while attorneys' time-recording and coding practices affect the basis for comparisons. Harvey and foundation-model providers are the subjects of competitive performance assessment. The article does not specify effects on employment, client fees or public access to justice.
